passages.text: Peter woke much earlier than his daily custom, came in to us, woke us, and said, “Let Faustinus and Faustinianus, together with Clement and the members of the household, follow me, so that we may go to a sheltered place by the sea and baptize her where no one can watch.” We went to the shore, found a calm, clean place among some rocks, and he baptized her. We brothers withdrew for the women’s sake, together with a brother and some others, bathed, and then came back and took the women with us. Going in this way to a hidden place, we prayed. Then, because of the crowd, Peter sent the women ahead, directing them to go by another road to the lodging, and permitted only us among the men to accompany our mother and those same women. We went to the lodging and spoke with one another while waiting for him to come. After a considerable number of hours Peter arrived, broke the bread with thanksgiving, put salt on it, and gave it first to our mother and then to us, her sons. Thus we dined with her and blessed God.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The source has singular ἀδελφῷ after the plural brothers. An additional fellow member of the community may be intended; he is left unnamed rather than silently omitted or identified as Peter.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν ἄρτον ἐπ’ εὐχαριστίᾳ κλάσας καὶ ἐπιθεὶς ἅλας
lexical_decisions.chosen: broke the bread with thanksgiving, put salt on it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The thanksgiving and salt are both explicit. The text is not supplemented with wine or made an explicit identification of a later eucharistic rite.

passages.text: Then, seeing that the crowd had come in, Peter sat down, told us to sit beside him, and began by explaining why he had sent us ahead from the baptism and had himself arrived late. He gave the following reason: “As soon as you withdrew,” he said, “an old laborer came in with us, inquisitively concealing himself. Having watched us beforehand, as he later admitted, to see what we would do when we entered the sheltered place, he came out secretly and followed. At a suitable place he approached, greeted me, and said, ‘I have followed you for a long time, wanting to speak with you, but I was ashamed, lest you be angry at me for being inquisitive. Now, if you wish, I will tell you what seems true to me.’ I answered, ‘Tell us what you think is good, and we will welcome you, even if what is said is not actually good, since with a good intention you have wanted to say what seems good to you.’”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The reflexive use of “steal” means hiding or stealing along rather than theft of property. The note preserves the figurative wording’s furtiveness.
The object is the man, not necessarily an endorsement of the truth of his statement, as the following concession makes clear.

passages.text: “The old man began speaking in this way: ‘When I saw that you had bathed in the sea and withdrawn to the hidden place, I secretly approached and watched to see what you would do on entering a concealed place. When I saw you praying, I withdrew. Pitying you, however, I waited so that I might speak to you as you came out and persuade you not to be deceived. For there is neither God nor providence; everything is subject to destiny assigned at birth. I am fully convinced of this from what I have suffered, having studied the discipline carefully for a long time. So do not be deceived, child. Whether you pray or not, you are bound to suffer what comes from natal destiny. For if prayers or doing good had any power, I myself would be in better circumstances. Now, if this poor clothing of mine does not mislead you, you will not disbelieve what I say. Once, when I had great material abundance, I sacrificed much to the gods and provided much for the needy; yet, though I prayed and acted reverently, I could not escape what was fated.’ I said, ‘What have you suffered?’ He answered, ‘There is no need to speak of it now. Perhaps at the end you will hear who I am, whose family I belong to, and in what circumstances of life I have come to be. For now I want you to be fully convinced that everything is subject to natal destiny.’”

lexical_decisions.chosen: destiny assigned at birth / natal destiny
lexical_decisions.rationale: γένεσις literally refers to birth or origin; in this discussion it denotes fate inferred from a nativity or astrological birth configuration. The later explicit reference to astrology supports this contextual rendering, not a blanket substitution for every use of the word.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὔτε γὰρ θεός ἐστιν οὔτε πρόνοια
lexical_decisions.chosen: For there is neither God nor providence
lexical_decisions.rationale: The denial is the old man’s stated position, not an assertion added by the narrator or translator.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τίς τε ὢν ἐγὼ καὶ τίνων
lexical_decisions.chosen: who I am, whose family I belong to
lexical_decisions.rationale: The elliptical plural genitive can concern ancestry or kin. It is not supplied as a particular named family.

passages.text: “I said, ‘If everything is subject to natal destiny and you are fully convinced that this is so, your advice reflects thoughts contrary to your own. For if even thinking cannot occur contrary to natal destiny, why do you labor in vain, advising that something happen which cannot happen? Moreover, even if natal destiny has existence, do not hurry to persuade me not to worship the master of the stars as well, at whose will even what is not to happen can happen. For what is subordinate must always obey its ruler. Worshiping the supposed gods, however, is superfluous if natal destiny prevails. For nothing happens contrary to what seems good to fate, nor can they themselves do anything, being subject to their universal natal destiny. If natal destiny exists, it is incompatible with not ruling first. It cannot be subordinate, since, being ungenerated, it has nothing older than itself.’”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ θέλοντος καὶ μὴ γενέσθαι τι, γενέσθαι δυνατόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: at whose will even what is not to happen can happen
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes the negated infinitive as characterizing an event not otherwise destined to happen; the final γενέσθαι then states that it can happen at the ruler’s will. This supplies the contextual relation to destiny in English, not a Greek emendation. Another possible linkage places μὴ γενέσθαι directly within what the ruler wills: “when he wills even that something not happen, its happening is possible.” That is more difficult in the argument, but the negation’s attachment is not uniquely established here. The main text does not omit either occurrence of “happen” or the negative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ γένεσις ἐστιν, ἀντίκειται τὸ μὴ πρῶτον ἄρχειν. ὑποκεῖσθαι οὐ δύναται ὡς ἀγένητον ἑαυτοῦ πρεσβύτερον μηδὲν ἔχον
lexical_decisions.chosen: If natal destiny exists, it is incompatible with not ruling first. It cannot be subordinate, since, being ungenerated, it has nothing older than itself
lexical_decisions.rationale: The conditional is retained. The nearest named referent is natal destiny, read as the ungenerated principle hypothesized by fatalism. The neuter ἀγένητον can refer to an understood principle rather than agree directly with feminine γένεσις. A reference back to God or an ungenerated divine principle is also possible and would change which ruler is said to be unsubordinated. The pronoun “it” deliberately does not add a noun identifying the unexpressed subject uniquely.

passages.text: “As we were saying such things to one another, a large crowd gathered. Then, looking at the crowd, I said, ‘I and my people have inherited from our ancestors the worship of God and have a command not to attend to natal destiny—I mean the discipline of astrology. For this reason I have paid it no attention. Thus I am not experienced in astrology; I will explain the things in which I am experienced. Since I cannot refute natal destiny from the very science concerning natal destiny, I wish to demonstrate in another way that affairs are governed by providence, and that everyone will receive honor or punishment according to what he does. Whether now or later makes no difference to me, provided that everyone will certainly receive the consequences of what he has done. Here is the proof that natal destiny does not exist. If someone standing here lacks eyes, has a crippled hand, a lame foot, or some other bodily condition that has no possibility of returning to health and lies beyond every profession of healing—someone whom even astrologers do not profess to heal, because nothing of this sort has happened throughout the long span of time—and I, by petitioning God, provide the healing, when such a condition could never obtain correction through natal destiny: if this happens in this way, are not those who blaspheme the God who made everything doing wrong?’ The old man answered, ‘Is saying that everything is subject to natal destiny blasphemy?’ I answered, ‘Very much so. For if all people’s sins, acts of impiety, and licentious deeds come from stars, and the stars were appointed by God to do these things, so that they bring about every grievous thing, everyone’s sins are referred back to him who placed natal destiny in the stars.’”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The source denotes a people or tribe; its proper name is not supplied in the English.
This can refer to every promise or claim of healing as well as a healing occupation. The main text keeps the claim that the condition lies beyond professed healing ability.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁπότε ἐκ γενέσεως κατόρθωσιν τὸ τοιοῦτο οὐδέποτε λαβεῖν ἠδυνήθη
lexical_decisions.chosen: when such a condition could never obtain correction through natal destiny
lexical_decisions.rationale: The hypothetical demonstration’s premise is retained as Peter’s argument. No actual present healing or empirical validation is asserted by the translation.

passages.text: “The old man answered, ‘You have truly spoken greatly, but my own awareness stands in the way of all your incomparable proof. For I am an astrologer, and formerly lived in Rome. Becoming friends with someone related to Caesar, I knew precisely his natal configuration and that of his wife, and I observed their deeds actually fulfilled in accordance with their natal destiny. I cannot be persuaded by your argument. For the arrangement of her nativity was one that produces adulteresses who fall in love with their own servants and die in water abroad. And this is just what happened: falling in love with her own servant and unable to bear the reproach, she fled with him, went abroad, shared his bed, and perished at sea.’”

lexical_decisions.chosen: my own awareness stands in the way
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνείδησις can mean conscience or personal knowledge/awareness. His ensuing firsthand account supports awareness, not a modern clinical diagnosis.

The source’s servants have bonded status and belong to the women’s households. “Slaves” would make the legal ownership more explicit; “servants” follows the supplied POB policy while this note preserves ownership and dependency.
The word describes the configuration of the nativity, not a clinical disposition. “Horoscopic configuration” is the more technical alternative.

passages.text: “I answered, ‘How do you know that the woman who fled, after going abroad, married the servant and, having married him, died?’ The old man said, ‘I know the truth securely—not that she married him, since I did not even know that she was in love. But after her departure her husband’s brother told me everything about her love, and how, being honorable—being the brother, after all—he did not wish to defile the bed; and how the poor woman, desiring him but ashamed before him and of the reproach—for she cannot be blamed, since natal destiny compelled her to do and suffer these things—fashioned a dream, whether true or false I cannot say. For he said that she had said, “Someone appeared to me in a vision and ordered me to leave the city of the Romans immediately with my children.” Her husband, anxious that she and his sons should be safe, immediately sent them to Athens to be educated, together with their mother and servants, but kept with him a third, younger son, since the one giving the message in the dream had permitted that son to remain with him. After a long time passed without his receiving letters from her, and after he himself had sent to Athens repeatedly, he took me with him as more devoted to him than anyone else and went to search for her. So I willingly shared many hardships with him during the journey, remembering that in his former prosperity he had made me a partner in everything, loving me above all his friends. We sailed away from Rome itself, came to these parts of Syria, and put in at Seleucia. Not many days after we disembarked, he died in despondency. I came here, sold myself, and from then until now have provided my food through the work of my hands.’”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The question uses marriage explicitly and is not reduced to the earlier description of sharing a bed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ ἀδελφὸς ὁ τοῦ ἀνδρὸς αὐτῆς
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative narration then uses ambiguous pronouns concerning the honorable brother and the woman’s desire. The main text retains that person and those pronouns without harmonizing this with the prior assertion about a servant or identifying the two men as one.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὄνειρον εἴτε ἀληθῆ εἴτε ψευδῆ ἐπλάσατο οὐκ ἔχω λέγειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: fashioned a dream, whether true or false I cannot say
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can mean fabricated or fashioned. The following uncertainty about truth is retained, rather than replaced by a categorical claim that the dream was false.
The reflexive sale is explicit and is not softened to merely hiring himself out. The narrative does not identify a purchaser or legal arrangement.

passages.text: “After the old man said this, I understood from his account that the old man he said had died was your father. I did not want to compare your circumstances with his account until I had consulted you. But after learning where he was staying and telling him where I was staying, for accuracy’s sake I asked only this: ‘What was the old man’s name?’ He said, ‘Faustus.’ ‘And his twin sons’ names?’ He answered, ‘Faustinus and Faustinianus.’ ‘And the third son’s?’ He said, ‘Clement.’ ‘And what was the name of their mother?’ He said, ‘Mattidia.’ So, moved to tears by sympathy, I dismissed the crowds and came to you, so that after sharing the salt I might consult you about these things. I did not want to tell you before we partook of salt, lest, overcome by grief, you spend the day of baptism in mourning, when even angels rejoice.” While Peter was saying this, all of us were weeping with our mother. Seeing us weep, he said, “Now let each of you bear what has been said courageously through fear toward God. Your father did not die today, but long ago, as you yourselves said in conjecture.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃν ἔλεγεν τεθνάναι γέροντα, αὐτὸς ἦν (ἐξ ὧν ἔλεγεν) ὁ ὑμέτερος πατήρ
lexical_decisions.chosen: the old man he said had died was your father
lexical_decisions.rationale: Peter here identifies the reportedly deceased subject of the story, not yet explicitly the living speaker himself. The old man’s later identity is not read backward into Peter’s present assertion.
The concrete salt-sharing expression is retained in this meal context rather than made an unspecified conversation.

passages.text: When Peter said this, my mother could not bear it and cried aloud, “Alas, husband! Loving us, you yourself died without judgment, while we live, see the light, and partake of food.” As this single lament ended, the old man came in. Just as he was about to ask the cause of the cry, he looked at the woman and said, “Alas! What does this mean? Whom do I see?” He approached, looked more closely, was seen in turn, and embraced her. Both were fainting from sudden joy; though they wanted to speak to one another, they were seized with speechlessness from their insatiable joy and could not keep control. But after a little while my mother said, “I have you, Faustus, sweetest to me in every way! How are you alive, when just a little earlier we heard you were dead? But these are our sons: Faustinus, Faustinianus, and Clement.” When she said this, we three fell upon him and covered him with kisses, faintly recalling his appearance.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb may mean without discrimination, unreasoningly, or without a decision. In the lament it can also convey dying without a hearing or resolution. The main text retains the compact ambiguity and does not supply a tribunal or turn it into “undeservedly” as a settled claim.
The verb can denote dying or perishing. Their subsequent speech and embrace support deathlike faintness or loss of consciousness here, not actual death followed by resurrection.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀμαυρῶς πως τὴν μορφὴν αὐτοῦ ἀνεφέρομεν
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can mean bringing back or reproducing. Their childhood separation supports recollection of his appearance rather than verbally describing it for an unstated audience.

passages.text: Seeing this, Peter said, “Are you Faustus, this woman’s husband and the father of her children?” He said, “I am.” Peter said, “Why, then, did you tell me your own story as though it concerned someone else, speaking of hardships, grief, and a tomb?” My father answered, “Being related to Caesar and not wishing to become widely known, I recast the account in the person of someone else, so that my own identity would not be understood. For I knew that, if I became known, the local rulers would hear, summon me, and, doing what would please Caesar, invest me with worldly prosperity, which I had renounced. For, having judged those I loved most to be dead, I could not give myself over to life’s luxury.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The term concerns being made conspicuous or talked about. His intention is avoiding recognition, not a claim that he has escaped lawful punishment.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς ἄλλου τινὸς τὴν ἐξήγησιν ἀνετυπωσάμην
lexical_decisions.chosen: I recast the account in the person of someone else
lexical_decisions.rationale: The old man explains deliberate third-person presentation. No earlier part of his narrative is silently rewritten to anticipate this admission.

passages.text: Peter said, “You did these things as you had planned. But as for natal destiny, were you then insisting on it falsely, or were you affirming it as true?” My father said, “I will not lie to you: I was genuinely affirming natal destiny as something that exists. For I am not uninitiated in the theory. Besides, there was also with me an Egyptian man named Annubion, among the best astrologers. He became my friend at the beginning of my travels and declared the death of my wife along with our children.” Peter said, “Then are you now convinced by what has happened that the claims concerning natal destiny do not hold together?” My father answered, “I must set before you everything that comes into my mind, so that, hearing answers to these things, I can learn by these [points] of this refutation. I know that astrologers are wrong about many things but also tell the truth about many. So I suspect that, in what they determine accurately, they tell the truth, whereas, in what they get wrong, they do so through ignorance. Thus I suppose the discipline itself holds together, but they say false things through ignorance because not everyone can determine everything accurately.” Peter answered, “Hold back: perhaps in the things about which they tell the truth, they happen to hit upon it rather than speaking from precise knowledge. For some of the many things said are bound to turn out.” The old man said, “How, then, can one become fully convinced about this: whether what concerns natal destiny holds together or not?”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: περὶ δὲ γενέσεως ἄρα ψευδόμενος διισχυρίζου· ἢ ὡς ἀληθεύων ἐβεβαίους;
lexical_decisions.chosen: as for natal destiny, were you then insisting on it falsely, or were you affirming it as true?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two alternatives are both retained. ὡς ἀληθεύων can concern the speaker’s sincere claim to truth as well as actual truth; the father’s answer distinguishes sincerity from the theory’s validity.
The particle marks a tentative possibility or concern; the ensuing contrast is framed as a suspicion, not asserted as established astrological science.
ἄπεχε can be a caution to pause or refrain. “Consider whether perhaps” is a contextual alternative, but the main text retains the imperative’s restraint rather than treating the matter as proved.

source_issues.source_quote: ἵνα πρὸς αὐτὰ ἀκούων μανθάνειν ἔχω τοῖσδὲ τούτου ἐλέγχου
source_issues.issue: The sequence τοῖσδὲ τούτου ἐλέγχου is syntactically compressed: τοῖσδε is dative plural while “of this refutation” is genitive singular. The main text supplies only a bracketed generic head, “[points],” taking the dative instrumentally and the genitive as qualifying those implied points: learning by these points of this refutation while hearing replies to the doubts. Another contextual reading would refer to means or stages of refutation rather than particular points. The wording is not emended into a dative plural noun or described as an OCR error. The referential details remain uncertain and require independent review.

passages.text: While both were silent, I said, “Since I know the discipline precisely, but my master and my father do not know it in the same way, I would like, if Annubion himself were present, to hold a discussion in my father’s presence. For then the matter could become clear, with an expert holding the inquiry with another expert in the same field.” My father answered, “Where, then, can Annubion be encountered?” Peter said, “In Antioch. For I learn that Simon the magician is there, and Annubion, who follows him, is inseparable from him. So, when we get there, if we actually find them, the inquiry can take place.” After much conversation, filled with joy at the recognition and giving thanks to God, we turned to sleep when evening overtook us.

lexical_decisions.rationale: This refers to Peter in the ongoing discussion, not a newly introduced speech of the divine Lord.

lexical_decisions.chosen: an expert ... with another expert in the same field
lexical_decisions.rationale: The same-field relation is explicit; the translation does not certify the underlying astrological discipline as true.
The conditional prevents the planned inquiry from being reported as already conducted.
